# Esophageal hypermotility disorders

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the esophagus > Esophageal hypermotility disorders*

[Original Article Link](/library/0I0eYh)

---

## Summary

Esophageal hypermotility disorders are a group of uncommon conditions that include hypercontractile <u>peristalsis</u>, which is caused by vigorous esophageal contractions, and <u>distal esophageal spasm</u>, which is caused by premature esophageal contractions. While the precise etiology is unknown, the disorders are thought to be due to <u>autonomic dysfunction</u> of the <u>esophagus</u>. Consumption of hot/cold food, <u>stress</u>, and <u>gastroesophageal reflux</u> can trigger an acute episode of esophageal hypermotility, which typically manifests as intermittent retrosternal <u>chest pain</u> and <u>dysphagia</u>, predominantly to liquids (but also, in some cases, to solids). It is important to rule out more common <u>causes of acute chest pain</u> and <u>dysphagia</u> before considering <u>high-resolution esophageal manometry</u> (<u>HRM</u>) to confirm a diagnosis of esophageal hypermotility. Treatment is symptomatic and typically includes <u>smooth muscle</u> relaxants, such as <u>nitrates</u> and <u>calcium channel blockers</u>. A trial of <u>PPIs</u> may be considered, as <u>GERD</u> often accompanies esophageal hypermotility disorders and may even trigger an acute episode. Endoscopic <u>botox</u> injection into the esophageal body or the <u>spastic</u> segment may be considered if there is an inadequate response to pharmacological therapy. Long myotomy (endoscopic or surgical) may be considered as a last resort option.

---

## Definitions

Esophageal hypermotility disorders are caused either by hypertensive or premature esophageal contractions. [[2]](/library/uyYpS7)




* Hypertensive esophageal contractions: vigorous esophageal contractions with <u>distal</u> contractile integral (DCI) > 8,000 mm Hg/sec/cm (see ''Diagnostics'')

* Hypercontractile esophagus (<u>jackhammer esophagus</u>): hypertensive propagative esophageal contractions in which at least 20% of swallows have a DCI > 8,000 mm Hg/sec/cm

* Hypertensive peristalsis (<u>nutcracker esophagus</u>): an obsolete term according to the Chicago classification; previously used to describe hypertensive propagative esophageal contractions involving progressive <u>peristaltic</u> waves with an amplitude â¥ 220 mm Hg on <u>conventional esophageal manometry</u>  [[3]](/library/9bbNDH)[[4]](/library/uuYpGI)

* Premature esophageal contractions: contractions with a <u>distal</u> latency of < 4.5 seconds between them (see ''Diagnostics'')
* Distal esophageal spasm (<u>DES</u>; <u>corkscrew esophagus</u>): premature and uncoordinated nonpropagative esophageal <u>peristalsis</u> in at least 20% of swallows





> [!NOTE]
> Hypertensive and propagative esophageal contractions are seen in <u>hypercontractile esophagus</u>. Premature and nonpropagative esophageal contractions are seen in <u>distal esophageal spasm</u>.
